parts.latex:
The fourth term of a geometric sequence is 48.

The eighth term of the same sequence is $\dfrac{3}{16}$.

Find the possible value(s) of the common ratio and the corresponding first term(s).

solutions.latex:
Let $a$ be the first term and $r$ the common ratio.

Then
$$ar^3=48 \qquad (1)$$
and
$$ar^7=\dfrac{3}{16} \qquad (2)$$
Dividing (2) by (1),
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{ar^7}{ar^3}&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{16}}{48}\\\therefore\ r^4&=\dfrac{1}{256}\\\therefore\ r&=\pm\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
If $r=\dfrac{1}{4}$,
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3&=48\\\therefore\ a&=3072\end{aligned}$$
If $r=-\dfrac{1}{4}$,
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3&=48\\\therefore\ a&=-3072\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that the limiting sum of the series exists for the given domain.
Find the limiting sum of the series.

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is $r = \cos^2\theta$.

Since $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$,
$$\begin{aligned} 0 < \cos\theta &< 1 \\ 0 < \cos^2\theta &< 1 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ |r| < 1$, so the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{1-\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Show that the total distance, $D$, travelled by the ball is given by

$$D=\dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q}.$$

solutions.latex:
Initial height of the ball is $H$ metres.

The height after the $n$th bounce is the $n$th term of the geometric progression with first term $a=\dfrac{qH}{100}$ (the first rebound) and common ratio $r=\dfrac{q}{100}$, $0<q<100$.

Height after the second bounce:
$$\begin{aligned} h_n &= T_n=ar^{n-1} \\ h_2 &= \dfrac{qH}{100}\times\dfrac{q}{100} \\ &= \dfrac{q^2H}{(100)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to model height of bounce as a geometric progression, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the first term was given as $H$, which would make $h_2=\dfrac{qH}{100}$.

solutions.latex:
Total distance travelled may be modelled as the limiting sum of a geometric series, since $0<r<1$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= H+2(h_1+h_2+h_3+\cdots) \\ &= H+2\left(\dfrac{\frac{qH}{100}}{1-\frac{q}{100}}\right) \\ &= H+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100-q)}{100-q}+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H-qH+2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H+qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to simplify the expression involving the limiting sum, or equivalent merit

329.stem:
A brand of rechargeable batteries provides power for 25 hours when first purchased fully charged.

After its first recharge it only provides power for a further 20 hours.

After its second recharge it only supplies power for 16 hours.

Each subsequent recharge after the second recharge results in the battery having 90% of its previous power available.

parts.latex: What is the available power after the third recharge?
What is the total expected battery life in hours?
If the battery is discarded when its power level falls below one hour after recharging, how many recharge cycles would it undergo before being disposed of?

solutions.latex:
After the 3rd recharge it will be $90\%$ of $16$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned} &= 16 \times 0.90 \\ &= 14.4 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

$$S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r} = \dfrac{14.4}{1 - 0.9} = 144 \text{ hours}$$
The battery will last
$$\begin{aligned} &= 25 + 20 + 16 + 144 \\ &= 205 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$T_n < 1$, $n = ?$
$$\begin{aligned} 14.4 \times 0.9^{n-1} &< 1 \\ 0.9^{n-1} &< \dfrac{1}{14.4} \end{aligned}$$
Taking logs of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} (n-1)\log 0.9 &< \log\left(\dfrac{1}{14.4}\right) \\ n - 1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{1}{14.4}\right)}{\log 0.9} \\ n &> 25.3152 + 1 \\ n &> 26.3152 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} n &= 27 + 2 \text{ previous charges} \\ n &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The power is less than $1$ hour after the $29^{\text{th}}$ charge.

The geometric series $a+ar+ar^2+\dots$ , where $-1<r<1$ , is such that the sum of all the terms after the $n^{\text{th}}$ term is equal to twice the $n^{\text{th}}$ term. What is the value of $r$ ?

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{a}{1-r}-\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}=2ar^{n-1}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ r^n&=2(1-r)r^{n-1}\\ r&=2-2r\\ 3r&=2\\ \therefore\ r&=\dfrac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$$

87.stem: Given the series $1\dfrac{1}{3}+2\dfrac{1}{9}+4\dfrac{1}{27}+8\dfrac{1}{81}\ \ldots$ . Find the expression of the:

parts.latex: general term.
sum.

solutions.latex:
Each term is a whole number plus a fraction:
$$1+\dfrac13,\quad 2+\dfrac19,\quad 4+\dfrac1{27},\quad 8+\dfrac1{81},\ \ldots$$
The whole numbers $1,2,4,8,\ldots$ form a GP with $a_1=1$, $r_1=2$.

The fractions $\dfrac13,\dfrac19,\dfrac1{27},\dfrac1{81},\ldots$ form a second GP with $a_2=\dfrac13$, $r_2=\dfrac13$.

So the general term is the sum of the general terms of the two GPs:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a_1r_1^{n-1}+a_2r_2^{n-1} \\ &= 1(2)^{n-1}+\dfrac13\left(\dfrac13\right)^{n-1} \\ &= 2^{n-1}+\dfrac{1}{3^n} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises two separate geometric progressions, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1}+\dfrac{a_2(1-r^n)}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1(2^n-1)}{2-1}+\dfrac{\frac13\left(1-\frac{1}{3^n}\right)}{1-\frac13} \\ &= 2^n-1+\dfrac12\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \\ &= 2^n-1+\dfrac12-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \\ &= 2^n-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)-\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_n=2^n-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)-\dfrac12 \text{ or } \dfrac{2^{n+1}-3^{-n}-1}{2}$$

Sunya and Jonathan are playing a game. The spinner below is spun. If the hand lands on red then Sunya wins (and the game is over). If the hand lands on blue then Jonathan wins (and the game is over). If the hand lands on green then another spin is taken.

$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{10}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{3}{5}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Evaluate $256+128+64+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{8}$.

parts.latex:
Suppose the geometric series $x+x^2+x^3+\cdots$ has a limiting sum, $S$.

By considering the graph $y=-1-\dfrac{1}{x-1}$, or otherwise, find the range of possible values of $S$.

solutions.latex:
The limiting sum of a geometric series with $a=x$, $r=x$ is
$$\begin{aligned} S &= x+x^2+x^3+\cdots\\ &= \dfrac{x}{1-x} \qquad \text{where } -1<x<1\end{aligned}$$
Rewriting the given function:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -1-\dfrac{1}{x-1}=\dfrac{-(x-1)-1}{x-1}\\ &= \dfrac{-x}{x-1}=\dfrac{x}{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
So, the graph of $y=\dfrac{x}{1-x}$ is as shown.

\exfigure{1628_q30_s1}

When $x=-1$, $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

From the graph, when $-1<x<1$, $y>-\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\therefore\ S>-\dfrac{1}{2}$$

592.stem: A patient is undergoing a treatment involving repeated injections of $M$ milliliters of medicine, separated by regular time intervals of $t$ hours. Let $A_n$ be the amount of medicine in the body immediately after the $n^{\text{th}}$ injection, so $A_1=M$. While in the body, the medicine decays exponentially such that the amount left in the body right before the $(n+1)^{\text{th}}$ injection is given by $A_ne^{-t}$.

parts.latex: Find an expression for $A_2$, and show that $A_3=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t})$.

The patient is safe from side effects as long as the amount of medication in the body stays below $2M$ milliliters. Find the minimum value of $t$, to nearest minute, such that the patient is always safe as this treatment continues indefinitely.

solutions.latex:
Before each injection the amount is multiplied by $e^{-t}$, then $M$ is added:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1e^{-t}+M \\ &=Me^{-t}+M \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_3&=A_2e^{-t}+M \\ &=(Me^{-t}+M)e^{-t}+M \\ &=M+Me^{-t}+Me^{-2t} \\ &=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t}) \end{aligned}$$

$A_n$ is increasing in $n$, so for the treatment to be always safe we need $A_\infty<2M$.

$A_\infty$ exists since $0<e^{-t}<1$ for $t>0$ (geometric series, $r=e^{-t}$):
$$\begin{aligned} A_\infty&=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t}+e^{-3t}+\cdots) \\ &=M\times\dfrac{1}{1-e^{-t}} \\ &=\dfrac{M}{1-e^{-t}} \end{aligned}$$
We require $A_\infty<2M$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{M}{1-e^{-t}}&<2M \\ \dfrac{1}{1-e^{-t}}&<2 \\ \dfrac{e^t}{e^t-1}&<2 \\ e^t&<2e^t-2 \\ e^t&>2 \\ t&>\ln 2\text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
In minutes:
$$\begin{aligned} t&>\ln 2\times 60 \\ &=41.588\cdots\text{ mins} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=42\text{ mins}$$

799.stem:
As shown in the diagram, a sequence of squares is inscribed within a right-angled triangle $ABC$, where $AB=a$, $BC=2a$ and $\angle ABC=90^\circ$. The squares are arranged such that each square touches the hypotenuse $AC$ and the side length is labeled as $a_1, a_2 \dots a_n$.

\exfigure{1358_q29_1}

figures.cap: right-angled triangle ABC with right angle at B and a sequence of decreasing squares a1, a2, ... along BC touching hypotenuse AC
solution sketch: annotated triangle: a - a1 on AB, areas A1, A2, A3, BC = 2a

parts.latex: By considering similar triangles, show that $a_1=\dfrac{2}{3}a$.

parts.latex: Show that the areas of the squares form a geometric sequence. State the common ratio.
Find, in terms of $a$, the total sum of the areas of all the squares.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1358_q29_s1}
$$\dfrac{AB}{BC}=\dfrac{a}{2a}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The small triangle above the first square (vertical side $a-a_1$, horizontal side $a_1$) is similar to $\triangle ABC$ (corresponding angles, both right-angled):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a-a_1}{a_1} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ 2a-2a_1 &= a_1\\ 2a &= 3a_1\\ a_1 &= \dfrac{2a}{3} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Each square sits on the one before in the same way as in (a), so
$$a_2=\dfrac{2}{3}a_1,\quad a_3=\dfrac{2}{3}a_2,\ \ldots$$
Using (a), the areas are
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= (a_1)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}a^2\\ A_2 &= (a_2)^2 = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}a_1\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}\cdot\dfrac{4}{9}a^2 = \left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^2a^2\\ A_3 &= (a_3)^2 = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}a_2\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}\cdot\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^2a^2 = \left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^3a^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The areas of the squares form a geometric sequence with $r=\dfrac{4}{9}$.
criteria: Shows successive areas, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The areas form a geometric series with first term $A_1=\dfrac{4}{9}a^2$ and $r=\dfrac{4}{9}$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum is $S_\infty=\dfrac{A_1}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{\frac{4}{9}a^2}{1-\frac{4}{9}}\\ &= \dfrac{4}{5}a^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the limiting sum formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The first term of an geometric series is 4 and the third term is 9. The common ratio is negative.

The 40$^{\text{th}}$ term of the series is given by:

solutions.latex:
$a = 4$; let the first three terms be $4, x, 9$. In a geometric sequence consecutive ratios are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{4} &= \dfrac{9}{x} \\ x^2 &= 36 \\ x &= \pm 6 \end{aligned}$$
The ratio is negative, so $x = -6$.
$$r = \dfrac{-6}{4} = -1.5$$
Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$T_{40} = 4 \times (-1.5)^{39}$$

parts.latex: Consider the geometric series: $1 - \tan^2\theta + \tan^4\theta - \ldots$
When the limiting sum exists, find an expression for the limiting sum in simplest form.
For what values of $\theta$ in the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ does the limiting sum of the series exist?

Quadratic inequalities.reason: Solving a quadratic inequality in tanθ; Year-11 wording overridden by owner ruling.

solutions.latex:
Each term is $-\tan^2\theta$ times the one before, so the series is geometric with $a = 1$ and $r = -\tan^2\theta$. Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{1}{1 + \tan^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta} \\ &= \cos^2\theta \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Two of: substitutes into $S_\infty$, uses $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$, simplifies $\dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta}$ (or one error), or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The limiting sum exists when $|r| < 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 &< -\tan^2\theta < 1\\ 1 &> \tan^2\theta > -1 &&(\text{multiply by } -1)\\ -1 &< \tan^2\theta < 1 &&(\text{rewrite}) \end{aligned}$$
$\tan^2\theta\ge 0$, so this means $\tan^2\theta<1$, that is $-1<\tan\theta<1$.

$\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$ and $\tan\theta$ is increasing on $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{\pi}{4} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

883.stem: A ball is dropped from a height of 2 metres onto a hard floor and bounces. After each bounce, the maximum height reached by the ball is 75\% of the previous maximum height. Thus, after it first hits the floor, it reaches a height of 1.5 metres before falling again, and after the second bounce, it reaches a height of 1.125 metres before falling again. Correct answers to 4 significant figures.

parts.latex: Find the maximum height reached after the fifth bounce.
Find the total distance travelled by the ball from the time \underline{after} reaching the maximum height with the 5\textsuperscript{th} bounce.

solutions.latex:
Let $h_n$ be the height after the $n$th bounce. Each bounce multiplies the height by $0.75$:
$$\begin{aligned} h_1&=2\times 0.75=1.5\\ h_2&=2\times 0.75^2=1.125\\ h_3&=2\times 0.75^3\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ h_5&=2\times 0.75^5\\ &=0.474609375\\ &=0.4746 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
Downward motion:
$$2+2\times 0.75+2\times 0.75^2+\dots+2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6+\dots$$
From $2\times 0.75^5$ on, this is a geometric series with $a=2\times 0.75^5$ and $r=0.75$; $|r|<1$, so the limiting sum exists.

Upward motion:
$$2\times 0.75+2\times 0.75^2+\dots+2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6+\dots$$
From $2\times 0.75^6$ on, this is a geometric series with $a=2\times 0.75^6$ and $r=0.75$; $|r|<1$, so the limiting sum exists.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance after 5th bounce}&=\dfrac{2\times 0.75^5}{1-0.75}+\dfrac{2\times 0.75^6}{1-0.75}\\ &=\dfrac{2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6}{0.25}\\ &=3.3222\ldots\\ &\approx 3.322 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the upward limiting sum, or equivalent merit
Finds the downward limiting sum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A YouTuber predicts that every person who views their latest video will share it with 5 other people after a day.

The YouTuber shares the video to 8 people in the first day.

After how many whole days should the YouTuber reach 1 million unique views?

solutions.latex:
This is a geometric progression with $a=8$ and $r=5$.

1 million unique views requires the sum of the geometric progression. Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000000&=\dfrac{8(5^n-1)}{4}\\ 1000000&=2(5^n-1)\\ 5^n-1&=500000\\ 5^n&=500001\\ n\ln 5&=\ln 500001\\ n&=\dfrac{\ln 500001}{\ln 5}\\ &=8.1533\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Therefore it takes 9 full days to reach 1 million unique views.
criteria: Correctly solves the required equation using logarithm laws, or equivalent merit
Identifies that a sum of a geometric progression is required and obtains the equation $1000000=\dfrac{8(5^n-1)}{4}$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly determines the number of days after solving the geometric progression equation using logarithm laws

parts.latex:
Consider the following geometric sequence

$$81,a,b,3$$

Find the value of $b-a$

solutions.latex:
The first term is $81$ and the fourth term is $81r^3=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}81r^3&=3\\ r^3&=\dfrac{1}{27}\\ r&=\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
So $a=81\times\dfrac{1}{3}=27$ and $b=27\times\dfrac{1}{3}=9$.
$$b-a=9-27=-18$$

parts.latex:
Using the value of $A$ found in part (a), show that the series

$$\Big(1+\cos A\Big)+\dfrac{1}{2}+\Big(1-\cos A\Big)+\cdots$$

has a limiting sum.

solutions.latex:
$T_1$, $T_2$, $T_3$ are geometric, so $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos A}&=\dfrac{1-\cos A}{\frac{1}{2}}\\ 1-\cos^2 A&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \cos^2 A&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\ \cos A&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$A$ is an angle in a triangle, so $0<A<\pi$:
$$A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ or } A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
Since $T_1>T_2>T_3$, the ratio $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}<1$.

If $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{6}}=\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}}\approx 0.2679<1$$
If $A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$:
$$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}}=\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{3}}\approx 3.73>1$$
$$\therefore A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ only}$$
criteria: Finds $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ (other potential solutions include $A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $\cos A=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$), or equivalent merit
Recognises a geometric series and writes $\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$ in terms of the cosine terms, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: fully correct solution, with due consideration of the possible quadrant for $\angle A$ and also $T_1>T_2>T_3$

solutions.latex:
With $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=1+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\ T_2&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}}\\ &\approx 0.2679<1\end{aligned}$$
Since $|r|<1$, a limiting sum exists.

parts.latex:
Determine the sum of the geometric series below.

$$2+6+18+\cdots+39\,366$$

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=2$, $r=3$.

Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$ to find the number of terms:
$$\begin{aligned}2\times3^{n-1}&=39\,366\\3^{n-1}&=19\,683\\3^{n-1}&=3^9\\\therefore n-1&=9\\n&=10\end{aligned}$$
Or: $n-1=\log_3 19\,683=9$, so $n=10$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{10}&=\dfrac{2(3^{10}-1)}{3-1}\\&=\dfrac{2(3^{10}-1)}{2}\\&=3^{10}-1\\&=59\,048\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The following sequence is geometric.

$$6-x,\qquad x-8,\qquad x+4$$

Determine the possible values of the common ratio.

solutions.latex:
For a geometric sequence the ratio of consecutive terms is constant:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x-8}{6-x}&=\dfrac{x+4}{x-8}\\(x-8)^2&=(6-x)(x+4)\\x^2-16x+64&=6x+24-x^2-4x\\x^2-16x+64&=-x^2+2x+24\\2x^2-18x+40&=0\\2(x^2-9x+20)&=0\\2(x-4)(x-5)&=0\\\therefore x&=4\text{ or }5\end{aligned}$$
When $x=4$:
$$r=\dfrac{4-8}{6-4}=-2$$
When $x=5$:
$$r=\dfrac{5-8}{6-5}=-3$$
$\therefore$ the possible common ratios are $-2$ and $-3$.
criteria: Equates the ratios $\dfrac{x-8}{6-x}=\dfrac{x+4}{x-8}$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: CFPE allowed for the common ratios. Only $\dfrac{1}{2}$ of the last mark was awarded if $r$ was worked out but it was concluded that $r=4$ or $5$.

parts.latex:
The sum of an infinite geometric series, with positive terms, is 3.

The sum of the cubes of its terms is $\dfrac{27}{19}$. What is the common ratio of the original series?

solutions.latex:
Let the sum of the original geometric series be $S_1$ and the new series (the cubes, first term $a^3$, ratio $r^3$) be $S_2$.
$$S_1=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=3\text{, so }a=3(1-r)\qquad(1)$$
$$S_2=\dfrac{a^3}{1-r^3}=\dfrac{27}{19}\qquad(2)$$
Substitute (1) into (2) and divide both sides by 27:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\big(3(1-r)\big)^3}{1-r^3}&=\dfrac{27}{19}\\\dfrac{(1-r)^3}{(1-r)(1+r+r^2)}&=\dfrac{1}{19}\\\dfrac{1-2r+r^2}{1+r+r^2}&=\dfrac{1}{19}\\6r^2-13r+6&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore r=\dfrac{3}{2}\text{ or }\dfrac{2}{3}$$
Since $|r|<1$ for a limiting sum:
$$\therefore r=\dfrac{2}{3}$$
criteria: Writes $\dfrac{a^3}{1-r^3}=\dfrac{27}{19}$ for the series of cubes, or equivalent merit

1109.stem:
A lake contains an initial population of 500 000 fish at the beginning of 2025. Each year, the fish population increases by 7% due to natural reproduction. After this increase, a fishing company catches fish from the lake. In 2025, 2000 fish are caught. In each subsequent year, the number of fish caught increases by 9% compared to the previous year.

Let $F_n$ be the number of fish remaining in the lake after the nth year's catch.

parts.latex: If the fishing was allowed to continue at this rate, find the year which there will be no fish in this lake.

meta.top_criterion_original: all steps shown ($F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$). Just putting $F_1$ or $F_2$ was not accepted.
meta.marker_note: All steps ($F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$) must be shown; just putting $F_1$ or $F_2$ was not accepted.

solutions.latex:
Continuing the pattern from part (i):
$$F_n=500000(1.07)^n-2000\left(1.07^{n-1}+1.07^{n-2}(1.09)+1.07^{n-3}(1.09)^2+\cdots+1.09^{n-1}\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with first term $1.07^{n-1}$, ratio $\dfrac{1.09}{1.07}$ and $n$ terms. There are no fish left when $F_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}500000(1.07)^n&=2000\left(\dfrac{1.07^{n-1}\left(\left(\frac{1.09}{1.07}\right)^n-1\right)}{\frac{1.09}{1.07}-1}\right)\\500000(1.07)^n&=2000\left(\dfrac{\frac{1.07^n}{1.07}\left(\left(\frac{1.09}{1.07}\right)^n-1\right)}{\frac{1.09-1.07}{1.07}}\right)\\500(1.07)^n&=100\left(1.07^n\left(\left(\dfrac{1.09}{1.07}\right)^n-1\right)\right)\\5(1.07)^n&=1.07^n\left(\dfrac{1.09^n}{1.07^n}\right)-1.07^n\\6(1.07)^n&=1.09^n\\6&=\left(\dfrac{1.09}{1.07}\right)^n\\\ln 6&=n\ln\left(\dfrac{1.09}{1.07}\right)\\n&=\dfrac{\ln 6}{\ln\left(\frac{1.09}{1.07}\right)}\\&=96.75\end{aligned}$$
The fish run out during the 97th year, and $n=1$ is 2025.

$\therefore$ Year 2121
criteria: Writes the expression for $F_n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: For a geometric series the third term $(T_3)$ is 1 and the sixth term $(T_6)$ is 27.
Find the common ratio.
Find the sum of the terms from $T_{10}$ to $T_{20}$ inclusive.

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3=ar^2&=1\\a&=\dfrac{1}{r^2}\qquad(1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}T_6=ar^5&=27\\a&=\dfrac{27}{r^5}\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Equating $(1)$ and $(2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{r^2}&=\dfrac{27}{r^5}\\ \dfrac{r^5}{r^2}&=27\\r^3&=27\\r&=3\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $(1)$:
$$a=\dfrac{1}{3^2}=\dfrac{1}{9}$$
criteria: Writes equations $(1)$ and $(2)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The terms from $T_{10}$ to $T_{20}$ sum to $S_{20}-S_9$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{a\left(r^n-1\right)}{r-1}$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{9}$ and $r=3$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}S_{20}-S_9&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{9}\left(3^{20}-1\right)}{3-1}-\dfrac{\frac{1}{9}\left(3^{9}-1\right)}{3-1}\\&=\dfrac{3^{20}-1-3^9+1}{2\times 9}\\&=\dfrac{3^{20}-3^9}{18}\\&=193\,709\,151\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $S_{20}-S_9$ with correct substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Consider the geometric series $1+\left(\sqrt{5}-2\right)+\left(\sqrt{5}-2\right)^2+\ldots$.

Find the exact value of the limiting sum, expressing your answer with a rational denominator.

solutions.latex:
A GP with $a=1$ and $r=\sqrt{5}-2\approx 0.236\ldots$

$|r|<1$, so the limiting sum exists.

Using $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ and rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}S&=\dfrac{1}{1-(\sqrt{5}-2)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt{5}+2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{3-\sqrt{5}}\times\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{3+\sqrt{5}}\\&=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{9-5}\\&=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: An arithmetic series has first term $a$ and common difference $d$ where $d\ne 0$. The 3rd, 7th, and 16th terms of the arithmetic series form the first three terms of a geometric series with common ratio $r$.
Show that $6d=5a$.
Find the value of $r$.

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$, the 3rd, 7th and 16th terms are $a+2d$, $a+6d$ and $a+15d$.

They are the first three terms of a GP, so the ratios of consecutive terms are equal:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{a+6d}{a+2d}&=\dfrac{a+15d}{a+6d}\\(a+6d)(a+6d)&=(a+2d)(a+15d)\\a^2+6ad+6ad+36d^2&=a^2+15ad+2ad+30d^2\\a^2+12ad+36d^2&=a^2+17ad+30d^2\\6d^2&=5ad\end{aligned}$$
$d\ne 0$, so dividing by $d$:
$$6d=5a\text{ as required}$$
criteria: Writes the terms as a GP, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is the 7th term divided by the 3rd term:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{a+6d}{a+2d}\\&=\dfrac{a+6d}{\frac{1}{3}(3a+6d)}\\&=3\times\dfrac{a+6d}{3a+6d}\end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $6d=5a$:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=3\times\dfrac{a+5a}{3a+5a}\\&=3\times\dfrac{6a}{8a}\\&=\dfrac{18}{8}\\&=\dfrac{9}{4}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Consider the geometric series

$$1+\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)+\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)^3+\ldots$$
Show with calculations why this geometric series has a limiting sum.

solutions.latex:
Each term is the previous term multiplied by $\sqrt{11}-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\sqrt{11}-3\\ &=0.31662\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$-1<0.31662\ldots<1$, so $|r|<1$.

$\therefore$ the GP has a limiting sum.

Using $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=1$ and $r=\sqrt{11}-3$, then rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4-\sqrt{11}}\times\dfrac{4+\sqrt{11}}{4+\sqrt{11}}\\ &=\dfrac{4+\sqrt{11}}{5}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: An amount of \$6000 is invested at an interest rate of 6.5% p.a. compounded annually. How much interest, to the nearest dollar, has been earned after 15 years?

$$\begin{aligned} A &= P(1+r)^n \\ &= 6000(1.065)^{15} \\ &= 15431.0\ldots \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The jump lengths are $180,\ 135,\ 101.25,\ \ldots$

The sequence is geometric with $a=180$, $r=0.75$, $n=10$. Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_{10}&=180(0.75)^{10-1}\\&=13.51524353\\&\approx 13.52\text{ cm (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: A farmer is monitoring the salinity of a dam on his property.  On the first day of observations, the salinity is measured as 0.15 ppt (parts per thousand).  Each subsequent day, the salinity increases by 2% of the previous day’s measurement.  When the measurement exceeds 10 ppt, the water will no longer be suitable for livestock and the farmer will begin to treat the dam.  On which day will the farmer need to start treating his dam?

solutions.latex:
The measurements $0.15,\ 0.153,\ 0.15606,\ \ldots$ form a geometric sequence with $a=0.15$, $r=1.02$.

The salinity reaches 10 ppt when $T_n=ar^{n-1}=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}10&=0.15(1.02)^{n-1}\\\dfrac{200}{3}&=(1.02)^{n-1}\\\log_{1.02}\left(\dfrac{200}{3}\right)&=n-1\\n-1&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{200}{3}\right)}{\ln(1.02)} &&(\text{change of base})\\n&=213.078176\end{aligned}$$
$n$ is a whole number, so the salinity first exceeds 10 ppt on day 214.

$\therefore$ the farmer needs to start treating the dam on the $214$th day.

1235.stem:
A company starts a page on social media.  Initially, the page has 200 followers $(ie\ T_0=200)$.  Each day the page gains an extra 200 followers but loses 10% of the number of followers on the previous day.

Let $T_n$ be the number of followers on the $n$th day.

parts.latex: Write a recurrence relation for $T_n$.
Show that $T_n=2000\left(1-(0.9)^{n+1}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Each day the page keeps $90\%$ of the previous day's followers and gains 200:
$$T_n=200+0.9\times T_{n-1}$$
where $T_0=200$ and $n\ge 1$.

$$\begin{aligned}T_0&=200\\T_1&=200+0.9\times T_0\\&=200+0.9\times 200\\T_2&=200+0.9\times T_1\\&=200+0.9\times(200+0.9\times 200)\\&=200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2\\T_3&=200+0.9\times T_2\\&=200+0.9\times(200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2)\\&=200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2+200\times 0.9^3\end{aligned}$$
Each term is the sum of a geometric series with $a=200$, $r=0.9$ and $n+1$ terms, using $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ T_n&=\dfrac{200(1-(0.9)^{n+1})}{1-0.9}\\&=2000(1-(0.9)^{n+1})\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an expression for $T_3$ in terms of powers of $0.9$, or equivalent merit

The first term is $a=T_1=6\cos\theta$ with $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, and the ratio is $r=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$:

$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{2\left(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}-2\right)}{-3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\left(\frac{1}{2}-2\right)}{-3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{-3}{-3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists, $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{-3\sqrt{3}}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{-9}{\sqrt{3}-1}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}+1} \\ &= \dfrac{-9\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right)}{2} \\ &= -\dfrac{9}{2}\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: An investment of \$4000 earns interest at a rate of $r\%$ p.a. over a period of one year. How much more interest would the investment earn, if interest is compounded half-yearly rather than yearly? Find the answer in terms of $r$.

solutions.latex:
With yearly compounding at $\dfrac{r}{100}$:
$$A_1=4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}\right)$$
With half-yearly compounding the rate per half-year is $\dfrac{r}{200}$, for $2$ periods:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= 4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{200}\right)^2 \\ &= 4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}+\dfrac{r^2}{40000}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The extra interest is
$$\begin{aligned} A_2-A_1 &= 4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}+\dfrac{r^2}{40000}\right)-4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}\right) \\ &= 4000\cdot\dfrac{r^2}{40000} \\ &= \dfrac{r^2}{10} \end{aligned}$$
So the investment earns $\$\dfrac{r^2}{10}$ more.

1906.stem: Consider the series $\ln x-3(\ln x)^2+9(\ln x)^3+\cdots$

parts.latex: Show that these terms form a geometric series.
Hence, or otherwise, find the values of $x$ for which the series has a limiting sum.

solutions.latex:
A series is geometric when the ratio of consecutive terms is constant.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} &= \dfrac{-3(\ln x)^2}{\ln x} = -3\ln x \\ \dfrac{T_3}{T_2} &= \dfrac{9(\ln x)^3}{-3(\ln x)^2} = -3\ln x \end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so the series is geometric with $a=\ln x$ and $r=-3\ln x$.

A geometric series has a limiting sum when $|r|<1$, with $r=-3\ln x$. The terms need $x>0$ and the series needs $\ln x\ne 0$ (for $x=1$ every term is $0$, so there is no ratio).
$$\begin{aligned} |-3\ln x| &< 1 \\ -1 &< 3\ln x < 1 \\ -\dfrac{1}{3} &< \ln x < \dfrac{1}{3} &&(\text{divide by } 3) \\ e^{-\frac{1}{3}} &< x < e^{\frac{1}{3}} &&(e^{(\cdot)} \text{ is increasing}) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ e^{-\frac{1}{3}}<x<e^{\frac{1}{3}}\quad(x\ne 1)$$
criteria: Uses $|r|<1$ with $r=-3\ln x$, or equivalent merit

1908.stem: The third term in a geometric sequence 18 and the sixth term is 486.

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{ar^5}{ar^2} &= \dfrac{486}{18} \\ r^3 &= 27 \\ r &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Then $9a=18$.
